Airbnb's Brian Chesky on the classic management philosophy, and why he rejects it:

"Go through the list of great CEOs, almost none of them that I'm aware of do recurring one-on-ones... Jensen Huang does not do recurring one-on-ones, famously."

"I do think a CEO should meet one-on-one with your people. I don't think it should be recurring... If you wanna get time with me, get a meeting with me. If you wanna call me, call me. Bump into me, talk to me. But most of my recurring meetings are group meetings."

"If there's lots of one-way kinda sensitive topics, there's probably something wrong in the company... If we're having all these sensitive conversations, well, why are they so sensitive? Why can't other people hear about them?"

"If I have a one-on-one with you and you tell me there's a problem and we debate it and we say, 'Here's the solution,' we haven't consulted anyone else. So now we just made a decision and no one else helped, consulted, or knew how we made that decision."

"'Hire great people, trust them, let them do their job, stay out of the details, do recurring one-on-ones.' I don't believe any of that, and I wanna acknowledge that many great leaders do."

@bchesky w/ @sampjacobs

Figma's Dylan Field on why design is the new code, and where the value goes as models get better:

"If you believe that coding models will continue to get better, then you also believe that it's more outer loop architecture, the decisions you make about how to go build a system that matter, not the code itself."

"The code is material, and then the value rises to the top and that becomes brand, it becomes product design, your marketing, your point of view in the world, and I think overall your judgment calls and strategy."

"Product design is really at the center of a lot of that."

"For designers, they will have a bigger role to play if they step up. Not everyone will step up. Some people will be like, 'But I liked what I was doing.'"

 "Overall the way you'll shape products is through design."

@zoink w/ @sophiadew on @MTSLive

Active bond managers sell the dream of beating the index. Almost none of them do.

Over the past 10 years, nearly every category of active fixed income fund trailed its benchmark. Government intermediate funds: 100% underperformed. General government: 96%.

The edge top managers once had is gone too. The best-worst spread collapsed from 1.9% a year in the 2000s to 1.1% since 2020, per Apollo.

Public core fixed income is beta you are paying active fees for. Index it.

🚨 🇫🇷  🇮🇹  France’s Bond Risk Is Outpacing Italy’s by the Widest Margin in Euro History. A reversal that says a lot about France’s deteriorating fiscal credibility.

📈 Remember that in July 2012, at the height of the European sovereign debt crisis, Italy had to offer more than 400 basis points in additional yield compared with France on its 10-year government bonds. Today, French 10-year bonds offer roughly 30 basis points more than their Italian counterparts. Yet France remains significantly less indebted than Italy with public debt expected to reach around 118% of GDP in 2026 compared with 138% in Italy. That means that investors are increasingly focused on the future fiscal trajectory.

📊 France is expected to run a fiscal deficit >5% of GDP in 2026 compared ~3.0% for Italy. Italy is now running a primary surplus of ~1.2% of GDP while France still has a primary deficit of ~2.5%. This means that Italy can cover its public spending excluding interest payments with its existing revenues while France continues to borrow money before even paying interest on its outstanding debt. As you all know, fiscal sustainability depends just as much on a government's ability to control future deficits as it does on its current debt burden.

✅ However, it is important to keep in mind that Italy has certainly not become a model of fiscal discipline. Its public debt remains enormous, its debt-to-GDP ratio is rising again, and its structural growth remains weak. The Italian government is even considering allowing its deficit to rise back to 3.4% of GDP in 2027. The spread story is much more about France losing part of the confidence it had historically enjoyed. With ongoing budget difficulties, a fragmented parliament, and the April 2027 presidential election approaching, investors are struggling to identify a credible path toward fiscal consolidation.

➡️ France is losing part of the funding privilege it has enjoyed for decades.

*Bloomberg link: https://t.co/2i1N7ggEC9

tweets.text: Nvidia earns a big profit whenever it sells a GPU. Whoever buys that chip, however, does not incur an immediate cost because the purchase is treated as capital spending. Thus, while aggregate cash flows do not change, reported earnings still rise. This has pushed up profits margins in the tech sector.

thread_tweets.text: Data centers are somewhat different in that they employ so few people. An $8 billion datacenter could employ only 100 people once it is up and running. That's $80 million per worker. The capital-labor ratio in the economy is $700,000. So, the capital-labor ratio for data centers is more than 100x that of the broader economy. This has the effect of pulling down the labor share, leading to higher aggregate profits at the economy-wide level.
